options.1: $\Z$ is closed and — in the discrete metric — bounded, since every distance is at most $1$. So this is a direct test of whether closed and bounded is enough. Try covering it by the balls $B(n, \tfrac12)$ and ask how many you can discard.
options.2: It is bounded, and the question is whether it is closed and whether that would even settle it. Consider the cover by the sets $(\tfrac1n, 2)$ for $n = 1, 2, 3, \dots$ and ask what a finite subcollection could miss.
options.3: Everything the option says is true: $\rho$ is a metric, it is bounded by $1$, and $\R$ is closed in itself. That is exactly why it is worth examining — if closed and bounded were enough, this would be compact. Try covering with the balls $B(n, 1)$ for $n \in \Z$.

feedback.reconsider: Heine–Borel is a theorem about subsets of $\R^n$ *with the usual metric*. For anything else, go back to covers and try to build one with no finite subcover.

distractors.0: Correct, and the only one. $[0,1]$ is a closed bounded subset of $\R$ with the usual metric, which is exactly the situation Heine–Borel covers.
distractors.1: No. The balls $B(n,\tfrac12) = \{n\}$ cover $\Z$, and no finite collection of singletons covers an infinite set. Closed and bounded, and not compact.
distractors.2: No. The sets $(\tfrac1n, 2)$ for $n \ge 1$ cover $(0,1]$, but any finite subcollection has a largest $n$ and so misses everything in $(0, \tfrac1n]$. It is also not closed in $\R$.
distractors.3: No. $\rho$ is a genuine bounded metric giving the same open sets as the usual one, so $\R$ is closed and bounded in it — and the cover $\{B(n,1) : n \in \Z\}$ has no finite subcover. This is the cleanest demonstration that boundedness is not a topological property.

explanation:
## Why $[0,1]$ and nothing else

**Heine–Borel** says: a subset of $\R^n$ *with the usual metric* is compact iff it is closed and bounded. $[0,1]$ qualifies. The other three are chosen to break each part of the misreading.

**$\Z$ discrete** is closed and bounded and not compact. Cover: $\{\,\{n\} : n \in \Z\,\}$, every one of them open, no finite subcollection covering.

**$(0,1]$** is bounded but not closed in $\R$. Cover: $(\tfrac1n, 2)$ for $n = 1,2,3,\dots$. Any finite subfamily has a largest $n$ and misses $(0, \tfrac1n]$.

**$(\R, \rho)$ with $\rho = \min(|x-y|,1)$** is the sharpest one. $\rho$ *is* a metric, and it has exactly the same open sets as the usual metric — so the two spaces are indistinguishable topologically, and compactness is a topological property. Yet in $\rho$ the whole line is bounded. Conclusion: **boundedness is not topological**, so it cannot by itself be equivalent to anything that is. The cover $\{B(n,1) : n \in \Z\}$ has no finite subcover.

## What is true in a general metric space

$$\text{compact} \iff \text{sequentially compact} \iff \text{complete and totally bounded}.$$

*Totally bounded* — finitely many $\eps$-balls cover the space, for every $\eps$ — is the right strengthening of bounded. Each of the three failures above is a failure of exactly one part: $\Z$ discrete is complete but not totally bounded; $(0,1]$ is totally bounded but not complete; $(\R,\rho)$ is complete but not totally bounded.

## The habit

When a theorem has a named hypothesis — *in $\R^n$*, *with the usual metric* — that phrase is doing work. Heine–Borel without it is false, and the counterexamples are a line each.
